newsitem.title: UK: UK CBI, PMI surveys add to rate rise pressure.
newsitem.headline: UK CBI, PMI surveys add to rate rise pressure.

text.p: Buoyant June retail sales figures and a strong PMI services sector survey on Thursday provide further justification for an early UK interest rate rise to dampen consumer demand, analysts say.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's maiden budget on Wednesday did not go far enough to dampen consumer spending and Thursday's surveys were likely to increase the Bank of England's concern about consumption, they said.

"Because Brown did not exactly tighten policy on the consumers yesterday, the encouraging CBI figures suggest even more upper pressure on interest rates," said Mark Wall, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"We predict that the CBI and other surveys are going to look quite robust in the coming months."
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said 58 percent of retailers reported increased sales volumes in June compared with last year while 19 percent said they were down.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said the services sector grew at a slightly slower pace in June. The PMI business activity index slipped to a seasonally adjusted 62.9 from 64.2 in May but this was still the third highest reading since the survey began a year ago.

"The CBI survey was very strong," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse. "It points to an early windfall effect and is a hint of what is to come in the second half of the year -- we're going to find there is quite a boom on the high street."
He was referring to "windfall" gains totalling around 30 billion stg which millions of Britons will receive this year as mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks.
"The Bank must respond with a rate rise of at least a half point next week," Jeffrey said.

Official interest rates have been raised in each of the last two months to their present 6.5 percent level. The Bank of England's monetary policy committee, empowered by Brown to set interest rates, meets next week and will announce any changes to interest rates on July 10.
Wall said he expects the central bank to raise official rates by 25 basis points next week.
"I am sure the Bank would like to increase rates by 50 basis points, but sterling really ties their hands on this one," Wall said.
Brown told a news conference on Thursday that no-one could be happy with the rise of around 18 percent in sterling against other major currencies since last year and said he wanted to help exporters.
Analysts noted that the PMI survey showed companies reporting skills shortages, which could put additional upward pressure on inflation.
"The most worrying comment was that there were signs of skill shortages and this will tend to bid up wages eventually," Jeffrey said.
Simon Briscoe of Nikko Europe Plc said the PMI survey was a little weaker than expected and suggested that the pace of expansion might be easing.
"The markets will cling onto that hope in the face of the Chancellor's decision not to raise consumer taxes," he said.

"However, the Bank now realises that they alone are responsible for controlling the economy and this survey shows that there is pressure to raise rates in July or August -- prices charged are edging up, albeit modestly."
David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy said the PMI survey would provide some relief as any moderation in the service sector -- the main engine of economic growth -- was to be welcomed.
"Such is the new-found pessimism in the market, however, that it will take more than one set of data to change the perception that interest rates are set to rise sharply," he said.

John O'Sullivan of NatWest Markets said it was difficult to judge the CBI distributive trades survey, especially after pessimism in the May survey had been contradicted by a 1.1 percent rise in official retail sales data.
"At face value, June was a stronger month, with household goods (where volumes rose 2.2 percent in May) doing even better in June," he said.
"The natural conclusion to draw is that the Halifax windfalls which came through last month had a positive impact on discretionary spending".
